title: Discharge Teaching & Discharge Planning
summary: Providing comprehensive discharge education to ensure safe patient transition from hospital to home.
steps: Start discharge planning at ADMISSION — not the morning of discharge.
Assess barriers: language, health literacy, cognitive ability, social support, financial, transportation.
Involve family/caregiver in all teaching if appropriate (with patient consent).
DISCHARGE EDUCATION topics (MEDICATIONS + DIET + ACTIVITY + WOUNDS + SYMPTOMS to watch for + FOLLOW-UP = MDAWSF mnemonic):
M — Medications: new medications, changed doses, stopped medications. Side effects to watch for.
D — Diet: restrictions or changes (low sodium, diabetic, renal, etc.).
A — Activity: weight-bearing restrictions, driving limitations, sexual activity, exercise progression.
W — Wounds: incision/wound care instructions, dressing changes, when to contact surgeon.
S — Symptoms to watch for (return precautions): fever, increasing pain, SOB, bleeding, etc.
F — Follow-up: exact appointment date/time/provider/location. What to bring.
Use TEACH-BACK method to verify understanding.
Provide written materials at appropriate reading level (6th grade or below is recommended).
Document: topics taught, method, patient/family response, teach-back result.
safetyTips: Lack of discharge education is the #1 modifiable cause of preventable readmission.
30-day readmissions are scrutinized by CMS — thorough, documented discharge teaching is both clinical and regulatory.
Verbal education alone is insufficient. Always provide written take-home instructions.
keyTakeaways: Start at admission, not day of discharge
Written materials at 6th grade reading level

title: Teach-Back Method
summary: Using the teach-back method to verify patient comprehension of healthcare education.
steps: Teach the concept in plain, simple language first. Avoid medical jargon.
After teaching, use teach-back to verify understanding — NOT a test of the patient, but a check of your teaching.
Ask the patient to explain it back IN THEIR OWN WORDS:
CORRECT: 'I want to make sure I explained this well. Can you tell me in your own words how you'll take this medication?'
WRONG: 'Do you understand?' (Yes/No answer — not verify comprehension)
WRONG: 'Can you repeat what I said?' (tests memory, not understanding)
If patient cannot explain it correctly: reteach using different words, visual aids, or demonstration. Do NOT repeat the same explanation louder or faster.
Use show-back for procedural skills (wound care, insulin injection): 'Can you show me how you would do this?'
Teach in small chunks — 3 key pieces of information per session maximum.
Document: what was taught, teach-back question asked, patient response, reteaching needed (yes/no).
safetyTips: 'Do you understand?' is not teach-back. Patients say yes to avoid embarrassment — it does not verify comprehension.
Low health literacy affects 36% of U.S. adults. Plain language is not optional — it is standard of care.
Teaching a patient who is in pain, anxious, or sleep-deprived will not be retained — timing matters.
keyTakeaways: 'Tell me in your own words' not 'Do you understand?'
Poor teach-back = unclear teaching, not a dumb patient

title: Home Medication Teaching
summary: Teaching patients to safely self-administer and manage their home medications at discharge.
steps: Review each discharge medication with the patient and/or caregiver:
Name of the medication (brand AND generic if possible).
What it is for (indication in simple language).
How and when to take it (dose, route, frequency, with food or not).
Important side effects to monitor and report.
Special instructions (don't crush, take with water, avoid grapefruit, etc.).
Highlight NEW medications and CHANGES from prior regimen.
Teach patients how to safely store medications: room temp vs. refrigerator, away from children.
Discuss adherence strategies: pill organizer, phone reminders, pharmacy blister packs.
Teach what to do for missed doses (each drug is different — do not double-up without checking).
Identify patients on HIGH-ALERT home meds (warfarin, insulin, digoxin) — provide extra counseling.
Encourage patient to fill ALL prescriptions before leaving (or before the pharmacy closes).
Provide phone number to call with questions.
safetyTips: Medication non-adherence causes 125,000 preventable deaths per year in the U.S. Education is protective.
For anticoagulants: teach signs of bleeding and INR monitoring. For insulin: teach hypoglycemia recognition and treatment.
Do NOT assume the patient knows what a medication is for because they've been taking it for years — often they don't.
keyTakeaways: Name, dose, purpose, side effects for every medication
Special attention to HIGH-ALERT home meds

title: Activity & Restriction Teaching (Post-Discharge)
summary: Teaching patients about activity restrictions, return-to-activity progression, and when to seek care.
equipment: Discharge instruction sheet with specific restrictions
steps: Clarify activity orders with provider BEFORE teaching (restrictions vary by diagnosis/procedure).
Driving: most post-surgical patients cannot drive while on opioids or with restricted extremity use. Provide specific timeline.
Lifting restrictions: specify in exact pounds. Post-laparotomy: typically no lifting >10 lbs × 6 weeks. Post-cardiac cath: no lifting >10 lbs × 24h on access arm.
Ambulation: specify if walker/cane/crutches needed. Stairs assessment — can patient do them safely?
Work and school return: provide specific timeline or 'return to work slip' if facility policy allows.
Sexual activity: specific to procedure — post-cardiac: typically 2–4 weeks. Post-gynecologic surgery: typically 6 weeks. Post-ortho: highly variable.
Exercise progression: 'Light activity' → 'Moderate' → 'Full return' — provide specific milestones.
RETURN PRECAUTIONS (reasons to go to the ER or call provider):
Fever >38.3°C (101°F) | Uncontrolled pain | Wound opening/drainage | Shortness of breath | Chest pain | Excessive swelling or redness.
Provide 24-hour contact number and when to call 911 vs. the clinic.
safetyTips: Vague instructions like 'take it easy' are not safe discharge instructions — be specific.
Driving while on opioids is illegal in most states. Document that this was explicitly taught.
Return precautions must be given in writing — verbal alone is insufficient for safety and documentation.
